    Keynotes

    Invited Talk 1: Sara Tonelli (FBK)

    About: I am the head of the Digital Humanities Research Group at Fondazione Bruno Kessler in Trento, Italy. My main research interests focus on how toxic content spreads online, including fallacies, conspiracy theories, disinformation and trolling. I find particularly interesting analysing multilingual settings, where different narratives and rethorical strategies are used. I am also interested in assessing and measuring biases in LLMs and analysing how different factors such as annotators’ behavior and synthetic data can amplify them.
    I hold a PhD in Language Sciences from Università Ca' Foscari, Venice. I am currently serving as Vice President of the Italian Association for Computational Linguistics and Program Chair of EACL 2027. In the past, I coordinated the KID_ACTIONS project funded by the Rights, Equality and Citizenship Programme of the European Union, whose goal was to prevent and respond to children and adolescent cyberbullying through innovative monitoring and educational technologies. I am currently involved in different international projects within the Horizon Europe framework on the topics of democratic resilience, trust in digital environments and AI for good democracy practices
    Title: A Ten-Year Retrospective on Hate Speech Detection and Analysis
    Abstract: This year marks two major milestones: the 10th anniversary of WOAH and the ACL Test-of-Time Award honoring the first breakthrough paper on hate speech detection. Over the past decade, research on hate speech has evolved significantly across model architectures, taxonomies, dataset curation and ethical alignment. Yet, many early insights still hold true, and the core challenge remains far from solved. Drawing on existing scholarship and my own research, this talk provides an overview of a decade of progress and pitfalls before outlining key open challenges that demonstrate why critical work in content moderation still lies ahead.

    Invited Talk 2: Su Lin Blodgett

    About: I’m broadly interested in examining the social and ethical implications of natural language processing (NLP) technologies, and on creating more equitable, just, and empowering NLP technologies by centering people—who are inseparable from language—in technologies’ development and evaluation. My recent work has addressed principled evaluation and measurement, particularly of generative AI capabilities, behaviours, and impacts; understanding how people perceive and use generative AI; and supporting AI and NLP practitioners in their ethical work. I’ve also worked on using NLP approaches to examine language variation and change (computational sociolinguistics), for example developing models to identify language variation on social media. I approach my work from an interdisciplinary and sociotechnical perspective and draw inspiration from a wide range of disciplines, including NLP, responsible AI (RAI), human-computer interaction (HCI), and sociolinguistics.
    I was previously a principal researcher in the Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Ethics in AI (FATE) group at Microsoft Research Montréal, where I was also a postdoctoral researcher. I completed my Ph.D. in computer science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst working in the Statistical Social Language Analysis Lab under the guidance of Brendan O’Connor, where I was also supported by the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship. I received my B.A. in mathematics from Wellesley College. I interned at Microsoft Research New York City in summer 2019, where I worked with Solon Barocas, Hal Daumé III, and Hanna Wallach. I was named one of the 2022 100 Brilliant Women in AI Ethics.
    Title: The social and political functions of AI narratives
    Abstract: Marketing materials position generative AI models as smarter, faster, and more useful than ever. A substantial body of scholarship and journalistic reporting has characterized such discourses as hype and carefully examined language technologies’ capabilities, behaviours, and impacts, in pursuit of technologies that are less biased, safer, and more inclusive. In this talk, I’ll draw together my and other recent work to argue that NLP researchers need to interrogate not only technical artifacts but also the narratives surrounding them and the functions these narratives help perform—and moreover, that not doing so may both make it harder to contest harmful political and economic arrangements, and inadvertently enroll us in enabling them.

    Invited Talk 3: Zeerak Talat

    About: Zeerak Talat is a Chancellor’s Fellow (~Assistant Professor in the U.S.) in Responsible Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence at the Centre for Technomoral Futures and the School of Informatics at the University of Edinburgh, where they lead the ZEST Lab. They are also a faculty fellow at DAIR. They work on the intersection between machine learning, science and technology studies, and media studies. Their research centres decolonial and anti-capitalist critiques of ML and providing evidence that current ML methods (i.e., the mathematics of it all) are constructed in a way that naturally afford authoritarianism, colonialism, and forms of hegemony (i.e., white supremacy, patriarchy, ableism, and so on) and thinking about and developing ML methods that rethink the ways in which ML is applied to offer resistance to such notions.
    They did their undergrad in Computer Science and their master’s in IT & Cognition at the University of Copenhagen, and their Ph.D. at the University of Sheffield, and have done two post-docs at the Digital Democracies Institute, and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence.
    Title: The Children of Omelas: Reflections on a Decade of Practice in Automated Content Moderation

    Invited Talk 4: Sarah T. Roberts

    About: Sarah T. Roberts is a full professor at UCLA (Gender Studies, Information Studies, Labor Studies), specializing in Internet and social media policy and culture, and the intersection of media, technology and society. She is the faculty director and co-founder of the UCLA Center for Critical Internet Inquiry (C2i2), co-director of the Minderoo Initiative on Technology & Power, and a research associate of the Oxford Internet Institute. Informed by feminist Science and Technology Studies perspectives and by critical theoretical frameworks, she is keenly interested in the way power, geopolitics and economics play out on and via the internet and through digital technologies, reproducing, reifying and exacerbating global inequities and social injustice. She is the president of the Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) through 2027.
    Roberts is the author of Behind the Screen: Content Moderation in the Shadows of Social Media, and is known for her work and insight into social media and internet culture, politics, economics and society. She holds a Ph.D. in Information Science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, USA.
    Title: "We Start Worlds”: Risk, Rewilding and a Beginner’s Mind
    Abstract: In this talk, I reflect on 16 years of research and scholarship in spaces and addressing subjects that Marwick, et al., describe as "risky"; (2025). In the first part of the discussion, I describe the psychologically challenging nature of my work and my relative naiveté about any potential impacts of it at its outset, the fraught relationship of scholarly work to one's identity, the responsibilities I have felt to those who have informed my research and to the wider world, and what is at stake for researchers conducting work that challenges powerful technological, institutional, corporate and political hierarchies. I then move to a discussion of an in-progress attempt at creating/regaining a sense of personal control, leaning on an ethos of “DIO,” or “do it ourselves,” by developing my own nascent alternative-tech ecosystem, introducing an artistic praxis into my work and life, trying to find meaning and community through these activities, and embracing the frequently-uncomfortable paradox of working at a high level of expertise, on the one hand, while trying to develop new skills and ways of seeing that, first, require an acceptance of a status of beginner, learner and student (Eno & Adriaanse, 2025).
    Inspired by but wary of the pitfalls of the cultural framing of the “Maker” and concomitant movements (Hepp & Schmitz, 2023; Turner, 2018), but in relationship to and in dialog with the above, I consider both theoretical and practical efforts at reuse, recycling, repair, repurposing and rebuilding. Specifically, how might decentralized analog and digital communication technologies (e.g., LoRa; mesh networks; discarded computers) that localize human-manageable networks among small groups or collectives via hardware and software “homelabs,” skill-building and skill-sharing, and portable data and computational tools decoupled from the corporatized and captured internet(s), serve as potential forms or sites of resistance? I have heard terms such as “end times computing” or “apocalyptic computing” used here, although I am partial to the more hopeful concept of “rewilding the internet” (Farrell & Berjon, 2024) as applied more broadly, with its roots in ecology, and related concepts of permaculture and local production. This talk will not be prescriptive nor complete in nature; rather, I will speak from a place of vulnerability and honesty about issues I have seldom discussed publicly, in the hope of starting a dialogue with colleagues and peers about our health, our duties to self and to others, and how we can make a livable world for ourselves in the face of challenging times.
